new.q: What does LED stand for?
new.w: An LED is a diode that gives off light.
sol: LED = a one-way valve that glows when current flows the right way.

new.q: The end of a diode marked with a stripe or bar is the:
new.w: The bar is the cathode, the end current leaves.
sol: Think of the symbol as an arrow pointing into a wall.
The arrow (triangle) is the anode side; the wall (bar) is the cathode.

new.q: Why does an LED circuit need a series resistor?
o: Once the LED turns on, only the resistor limits the current
The LED needs extra voltage to start
The resistor makes the LED brighter than its rating
The resistor changes AC into DC
new.w: A lit LED has almost no resistance of its own, so something else must limit current.
sol: Picture a garden hose with no nozzle: the water just gushes.
The LED drop is nearly fixed, so the leftover voltage lands on the resistor and Ohm's law sets the current.
Without it, current climbs until the LED burns out.

new.q: A 5.0 V supply feeds a red LED (2.0 V drop) and a resistor in series. What voltage is across the resistor?
new.w: Series voltages add up to the supply, so the resistor gets what the LED leaves.
sol: Common slip: forgetting the LED uses up part of the voltage.

new.q: A 5.0 V source, a silicon diode wired backwards and a 1 kΩ resistor are in series. What is the voltage across the diode, in volts?
new.w: A reverse-biased diode blocks, so it takes the whole supply.
sol: Reverse bias widens the barrier, like a closed gate.
Almost no current flows, so the resistor has about 0 V (V = IR with I ≈ 0).
All 5 V must therefore appear across the gate: the diode.

new.q: A silicon diode is in series with a 5 V source and a 1 kΩ load, forward biased. The voltage across the load is about:
new.w: The diode takes about 0.7 V first; the load gets what is left.
sol: Think of the diode as a toll booth that always charges 0.7 V.
Mistake: assuming a conducting diode drops 0 V or the full supply.

new.q: A white LED (about 3 V drop) is tried on a 3.0 V coin cell with a resistor in series. Most likely it will:
o: stay dark or glow very faintly
light only when the cell is reversed
new.w: The drop alone nearly uses the whole supply, so little voltage is left to push current.
sol: Little voltage across the resistor means almost no current.
Picture a hill: the LED's 3 V climb eats all the height, leaving nothing to roll.

new.q: A microcontroller pin gives 3.3 V. A red LED (2.0 V drop) needs 5 mA. Find the series resistor, in ohms.
new.w: Leftover voltage divided by the wanted current.
sol: Convert mA to A first: 5 mA = 0.005 A.

new.q: A red LED (2.0 V drop) carries 20 mA from 12 V. Find the power used by the LED itself, in milliwatts.
new.w: Power = voltage across it × current through it.
sol: P = V × I for any part.
Do not use the supply voltage; only the LED's own drop.

new.q: A 9.0 V battery runs one LED at 15 mA through a series resistor. How much power does the battery supply, in milliwatts?
new.w: Source power = source voltage × total current. The resistor and LED share it.
sol: The current is the same everywhere in a series loop.
Trap: counting only the resistor or only the LED; the battery pays for both.

new.q: Three red LEDs (1.8 V each) in series with a resistor run at 10 mA from 9.0 V. Find the resistor in ohms.
new.w: Series drops add; the resistor takes what is left.

new.q: A 12 V supply and a red LED (2.0 V drop) with a maximum of 20 mA. What is the smallest safe standard resistor (E12: 330, 390, 470, 560, 680, 820)? Answer in ohms.
new.w: Calculate, then round UP to the next standard value so current stays under the limit.
sol: 500 is not on the list. 470 is below it, which allows more than 20 mA.

new.q: Using the 560 Ω resistor from a 12 V supply and a 2.0 V LED, what is the actual LED current in milliamps?
new.w: Rounding the resistor up gives a current a bit below the limit.

new.q: An LED (2.0 V drop) with a 330 Ω resistor each. Two such branches are wired in parallel from 5.0 V. Find the total supply current in milliamps.
new.w: Parallel branches each draw their own current; the supply gives the sum.
sol: Total = 18.2 mA. Like two taps on one water main: flows add.

new.q: A 5.0 V supply drives an LED (2.0 V drop) through a resistor. If the supply is raised to 10 V with the same resistor, the current becomes how many times larger? (give a decimal)
new.w: The LED drop stays about the same, so the resistor voltage grows by more than the supply does.
sol: 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67×. Doubling the supply does NOT double the current.

new.q: A 9 V battery rated 500 mAh powers one LED branch drawing 20 mA. About how many hours will it last?
new.w: Hours = capacity ÷ current. A series loop draws the same current from the battery as through the LED.
sol: Think of mAh as the size of a fuel tank.
The extra volts are burned in the resistor; they do not extend the time.

new.q: A 9.0 V supply, an LED (2.0 V drop) and a resistor. The LED must still get at least 5 mA to be visible. What is the largest resistor, in ohms?
new.w: A bigger resistor means less current, so there is a maximum value too.
sol: Any larger and the LED is too dim.

new.q: A 12 V battery feeds a 2.0 A motor through a series silicon diode that protects against reversed connection. How much power turns into heat in the diode, in watts?
new.w: Power = diode drop × current.
sol: The diode always drops about 0.7 V when conducting.
The protection is not free: the diode must be rated for heat and 2 A.

new.q: Two silicon diodes are wired in opposite directions in parallel, and this pair is in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5.0 V DC source. Find the current in milliamps.
new.w: Only one diode can conduct; the other is reverse biased. The pair holds about 0.7 V.
sol: Picture two one-way doors facing opposite ways: current uses the door facing it.
I = 4.3 ÷ 1000 = 4.3 mA. Drops do not add since only one diode is in the path.

new.q: A 9.0 V supply, an LED (2.0 V), one silicon diode (0.7 V) and a 470 Ω resistor are all in series. Find the current in milliamps.
new.w: Add every forward drop, then see what is left for the resistor.

new.q: A 12 V source feeds a 1.0 kΩ series resistor and a 5.1 V Zener diode connected in reverse breakdown. Find the current in milliamps through the Zener.
new.w: The Zener holds its voltage; the resistor takes the rest.
sol: Zener acts like a pressure-relief valve that clamps at 5.1 V.

new.q: The same 12 V, 1.0 kΩ series resistor and 5.1 V Zener now have a 1.0 kΩ load connected across the Zener. How many milliamps flow through the Zener?
new.w: The load takes part of the series current; the Zener gets only the remainder.
sol: Total current in the 1 kΩ series resistor = 6.9 mA.
Zener current = 6.9 − 5.1 = 1.8 mA. The Zener is the overflow drain; if the load takes it all, regulation fails.

new.q: A 10 V peak AC source feeds a single silicon diode and a load (half-wave rectifier). What is the peak voltage across the load, in volts?
new.w: The diode only conducts after it wins its 0.7 V toll.
sol: For the rest of the cycle, the diode blocks and the load sees about 0 V.

new.q: A bridge rectifier uses four silicon diodes. In each half cycle, current passes through two of them in series with the load. For a 10 V peak AC input, what is the peak load voltage, in volts?
new.w: Two diode drops (2 × 0.7 V) are lost on the way through.
sol: Path = in through one diode, through the load, back through a second diode.

new.q: Why do we always round a calculated LED resistor UP to the next standard value?
o: A larger resistor gives a smaller current, which keeps the LED within its limit
A larger resistor gives more current, so the LED is brighter
Standard values only come in larger sizes
It makes the LED drop voltage higher
new.w: Current and resistance move in opposite directions.
sol: Think of narrowing a pipe: less flow.
Rounding down widens the pipe, so current goes above the limit.
Rounding up only dims the LED slightly.

new.q: A forward-biased silicon diode's voltage changes from 0.65 V to 0.72 V. Which best describes what happens to its current?
o: It rises sharply, many times larger
new.w: Near the knee, a tiny voltage change causes a huge current change.
sol: The diode is like a steep waterslide after a flat start.
Voltage barely moves (about 0.7 V) while current ranges from mA to amps.
That is why a resistor is needed to set the current, not the voltage.

new.q: Two silicon diodes are both forward biased and wired in PARALLEL, then in series with a resistor. The voltage across the pair is about:
new.w: Parallel parts share the same voltage; their drops do not add.
sol: In parallel, two paths down the same hill: the hill is still 0.7 V high.

new.q: A relay coil is on a 12 V supply with a flyback diode across it. Which way must the diode face?
o: Cathode (bar) toward the positive side of the coil
Anode toward the positive side of the coil
In series with the coil, anode to ground
new.w: In normal operation the diode must block; only the coil's spike makes it conduct.
sol: Normal: positive at the cathode side means reverse bias, so no current.
Switch-off: the coil's collapsing field flips its polarity, so the diode now conducts and loops the energy safely.
Picture a heavy flywheel: it keeps spinning when you stop pushing, so give it a path.

new.q: A relay coil is switched off and a voltage spike appears across it. Why?
o: A coil resists sudden changes in current, so it pushes current even after the switch opens
The supply voltage doubles when the switch opens
The relay contacts create static electricity
new.w: Inductors oppose change in current, like water inertia.
sol: Water in a pipe keeps moving when you slam the valve, causing a pressure spike (water hammer).
The coil's magnetic field collapses and induces a large voltage.
Without a path, that voltage can jump a gap and damage the switch or transistor.

new.q: A 5.0 V supply drives an LED (2.0 V drop) with a 150 Ω resistor. Find the current in milliamps.
new.w: Resistor voltage over resistance.

new.q: A resistor limits an LED (2.0 V) to 25 mA from a 12 V supply. A 1/4 W (0.25 W) resistor is on hand. What is the best choice?
o: The needed 400 Ω resistor dissipates 0.25 W, right at the limit, so use a 1/2 W part
R = 400 Ω dissipates 0.05 W, so 1/4 W is plenty
R = 400 Ω dissipates 0.6 W, so use 1 W
new.w: Calculate the power, then leave a safety margin.
sol: P = I²R = 0.025² × 400 = 0.25 W, exactly the rating.
Parts running at their limit get very hot, so choose 1/2 W.

new.q: A solar cell or photodiode, when lit, can:
o: produce a voltage and push current through a load
only block current like an open switch
store charge like a battery for years
new.w: Light freeing charges in the junction is the LED process run backwards.
sol: Photodiode and solar cell: light in, current out.
The junction's built-in barrier sorts the freed charges.

new.q: Select ALL true statements about a forward-biased silicon LED or diode.
o: Current flows from anode to cathode
Its drop stays near 0.7 V (silicon diode) once conducting
It behaves like an open switch
new.w: Forward bias opens the gate: narrow barrier and current flows.
sol: It is NOT an open switch; that is reverse bias.
The drop is almost fixed, which is why a resistor sets the current.

new.q: Match each diode type to its main job.
pairs: Holds a steady voltage in reverse breakdown
Protects against a coil's voltage spike
new.w: Each diode type uses the junction differently.
sol: Flyback: safe loop for a coil's energy.

new.q: Order these LEDs by forward voltage drop, smallest first.
new.w: Shorter wavelength light needs a bigger energy gap, so a larger voltage.

new.q: A battery is connected backwards to a series LED and resistor. The LED:
o: stays off, since it is reverse biased
new.w: Reverse bias blocks the current.
sol: Think of a one-way door pushed the wrong way.
Only a tiny leakage current flows.
Ordinary LEDs can be damaged by large reverse voltage, so check polarity.

new.q: Which circuit part is the best simple choice to stop damage if a battery is connected backwards?
o: a diode in series with the supply
new.w: A series diode only passes current one way.
sol: Normal battery: it conducts but costs 0.7 V.
Like a turnstile that only spins one way.

new.q: What is the SI unit of capacitance?
new.w: Capacitance is measured in farads, named for Michael Faraday.
sol: Real parts are usually µF, nF or pF because a whole farad is huge.

new.q: A capacitor can best be compared to:
o: a small rechargeable bucket for charge
new.w: It stores charge and releases it later.
sol: Voltage is like the water level in the bucket.
Capacitance is how wide the bucket is: wider means more water per level.

new.q: Which capacitor type can be damaged by connecting it backwards?
new.w: Electrolytic caps have a + and a − side.
sol: The stripe on the can marks the negative lead.
Wrong polarity can heat the part or even make it burst.

new.q: Convert 4700 nF to microfarads.
Order these capacitances from smallest to largest.
new.w: Each prefix is 1000 times the one before.

new.q: A 220 µF capacitor is charged to 5.0 V. Find the charge in millicoulombs.
new.w: Q = C × V.
sol: Charge = how much water is in the bucket.

new.q: A capacitor holds 0.50 mC at 5.0 V. Find its capacitance in microfarads.
new.w: C = Q ÷ V.

new.q: A 1000 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V. Find the stored energy in millijoules.
new.w: E = ½CV².
sol: = 72 mJ. Square the voltage, not just double it.

new.q: A 2.0 mF capacitor is charged to 10 V. Find the stored energy in millijoules.
new.w: E = ½CV², careful with units.

new.q: A camera flash capacitor of 100 µF is charged to 300 V. Find the energy in joules.
new.w: Voltage is squared, so high voltage stores lots of energy.
sol: Even small capacitors can hold a lot at high voltage.

new.q: The voltage across a capacitor is doubled. Which statement is true?
o: The charge doubles and the energy quadruples
The charge quadruples and the energy doubles
new.w: Q = CV is linear in V; E = ½CV² is quadratic.

new.q: The voltage across a capacitor is cut to one half. The stored energy becomes:
new.w: Energy goes with voltage squared.
sol: Halving V halves the water level but the bucket's 'pressure energy' falls fourfold.

new.q: Three 10 µF capacitors are in parallel. Find the total capacitance in microfarads.
new.w: Parallel capacitors add, like adding bucket widths side by side.
sol: Plates in parallel behave like one big plate.

new.q: Four 8.0 µF capacitors are connected in series. Find the equivalent in microfarads.
new.w: Equal capacitors in series: C ÷ n.
sol: Series makes a bigger gap, so less capacitance.

new.q: Capacitors of 4.7 µF and 10 µF are in series. Find the equivalent in microfarads.
new.w: Product over sum works for two in series.
sol: Always smaller than the smaller one (4.7).

new.q: Three 10 µF capacitors are in series. Find the equivalent in microfarads.
new.w: Add reciprocals.
sol: Pattern: n equal caps in series give C/n.

new.q: A 10 µF capacitor is in parallel with a series pair of 6.0 µF and 3.0 µF. Find the total in microfarads.
new.w: Solve the series pair first, then add it in parallel.

new.q: A 20 µF capacitor is in series with a parallel pair of 10 µF and 10 µF. Find the total in microfarads.
new.w: Collapse the parallel pair first, then do the series.

new.q: A 12 V source is across a 6.0 µF and a 3.0 µF capacitor in series. Find the voltage across the 3.0 µF capacitor, in volts.
new.w: In series both have the same charge, so the smaller capacitor gets more voltage.
sol: C_eq = 2 µF, so Q = 2 µF × 12 V = 24 µC.
The 6 µF has 4 V. Small bucket fills to a higher level.

new.q: A 10 µF and a 22 µF capacitor are in parallel across 5.0 V. Find the total charge in microcoulombs.
new.w: Parallel caps see the same voltage; add the capacitances, then Q = CV.

new.q: What capacitor must be placed in series with a 6.0 µF capacitor to give an equivalent of 2.0 µF? Answer in microfarads.
new.w: Use 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ and solve.

new.q: A 10 µF capacitor is charged to 10 V, then disconnected. It is then connected across an uncharged 10 µF capacitor. Find the final voltage across the pair, in volts.
new.w: Charge is conserved; it spreads over twice the capacitance.
sol: = 5 V. Like pouring one bucket of water into two.

new.q: Same setup: a 10 µF at 10 V connects to an uncharged 10 µF. What is the total energy after sharing, in microjoules?
new.w: Energy is lost when charge shares (heat and spark).
sol: Half the energy is lost, even though charge is conserved.

new.q: A 100 pF air capacitor has its plate gap doubled. Find the new capacitance in picofarads.
new.w: C = εA/d, so C is inversely proportional to the gap.
sol: Plates farther apart feel each other less.

new.q: A 50 pF air capacitor has a dielectric with relative permittivity 4 fully inserted. Find the new capacitance in picofarads.
new.w: A dielectric multiplies C by its relative permittivity.
sol: The material cancels part of the field, letting more charge sit on the plates.

new.q: A parallel-plate capacitor has its plate area doubled AND its gap doubled. The capacitance:
new.w: C ∝ A/d.
sol: Bigger plates help; bigger gap hurts equally.

new.q: A capacitor is charged by a battery, then the battery STAYS connected while the plates are pulled apart. The charge on the plates:
new.w: The battery fixes V; C falls, so Q = CV falls.
sol: V is held by the battery.
Q = CV goes down: charge flows back into the battery.

new.q: A capacitor is charged and then DISCONNECTED from the battery. The plates are pulled apart. The voltage across it:
new.w: Charge has nowhere to go, so Q stays fixed; C drops so V = Q/C rises.
sol: V = Q/C goes up. You did work pulling opposite charges apart.

new.q: A 12 V battery, a 1.0 kΩ and a 2.0 kΩ resistor in series, with a capacitor across the 2.0 kΩ resistor. After a long time, find the capacitor voltage in volts.
new.w: Fully charged, the capacitor carries no current, so the resistors act as an ordinary divider.
sol: The capacitor just matches the voltage across its neighbor.

new.q: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 100 µF capacitor. Find the time constant τ = RC, in seconds.
new.w: τ is the time to charge about 63% of the way.
sol: After about 5τ it is essentially full.

new.q: After one time constant (τ = RC), a capacitor charging from 0 V toward 12 V has reached about 63% of the final voltage. Find that voltage in volts.
new.w: Charging slows down as the capacitor fills, like filling a bucket whose flow slows when it is nearly full.
sol: It does not fill linearly; each τ closes about 63% of the remaining gap.

new.q: A 16 V-rated capacitor is used on a 12 V circuit that sometimes spikes to 20 V. The best change is:
o: use a capacitor rated above the highest voltage, such as 25 V
use a capacitor with a lower rating
use the same part, spikes do not matter
new.w: Voltage rating is the maximum safe voltage, like a bucket's wall height.
sol: Above the rating the dielectric breaks down.
Spikes count, so pick above 20 V.
25 V is the next common size.

new.q: Select ALL changes that increase the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor.
new.w: C = εA/d.
sol: Area and ε on top increase C.
Gap d on the bottom: smaller d increases C.

new.q: Match each quantity to its unit.
new.w: Know each quantity and its unit.

new.q: Where is a bar magnet's field strongest?
o: near the poles, where field lines are closest
new.w: Crowded field lines mean a strong field.
sol: Picture people in a crowd: dense near the exit.

new.q: A magnet's field lines never:
new.w: Crossing would mean two directions at one point.
sol: A compass at any point points only one way.
So lines cannot cross, like single-lane roads.

new.q: A magnet is held still inside a coil. The voltage induced in the coil is:
o: equal to the magnet's strength in volts
new.w: Only a changing flux induces voltage.
sol: Like a stopped pendulum: no motion, no effect.

new.q: An ideal transformer has 500 primary turns and a 120 V primary. How many secondary turns give 24 V?
new.w: Turns ratio equals voltage ratio.

new.q: A step-up transformer must change 12 V to 120 V. The primary has 50 turns. How many secondary turns?
new.w: The voltage ratio sets the turns ratio.

new.q: An ideal transformer's secondary supplies 60 W to a load. How many watts does its primary take, in watts?
new.w: Ideal means no losses.
sol: Real ones lose a little as heat.

new.q: A transformer takes 100 W and delivers 90 W. What is its efficiency, in percent?
new.w: Efficiency = output ÷ input.
sol: The missing 10 W is lost as heat.

new.q: An ideal transformer steps 240 V down to 12 V. The load takes 5.0 A. Find the primary current in amps.
new.w: Power is conserved, so the high-voltage side has the lower current.

new.q: A wire 0.30 m long carries 4.0 A at right angles to a 0.50 T field. Find the force in newtons.
new.w: F = BIL.
sol: Force is at right angles to both.

new.q: A 0.50 m wire at right angles to a field carries 2.0 A and feels a force of 0.20 N. Find B in teslas.
new.w: Rearrange F = BIL.

new.q: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force F = BIL. If the current is doubled and the wire length is halved, the force:
new.w: F depends on the product I × L.

new.q: A transformer's primary is connected to a steady 12 V DC battery. After the first instant, the secondary voltage is:
new.w: No changing flux, no induction. A transformer is an AC machine.
sol: The primary may also overheat, since only its small wire resistance limits current.

new.q: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed toward a coil. By Lenz's law, the coil end facing the magnet becomes:
o: a pole that flips with each turn
new.w: The induced current opposes the change: it pushes the approaching magnet away.
sol: Pushing away needs like poles: N facing N.
If it attracted, the magnet would speed up and free energy appears, impossible.
Lenz's law is nature resisting change.

new.q: A strong magnet dropped down a copper pipe falls very slowly even though copper is not magnetic. Why?
o: The moving magnet induces currents in the copper that oppose its motion
Copper is attracted to the magnet
Air in the pipe supports it
new.w: Changing flux induces eddy currents; Lenz's law says they resist the motion.
sol: The magnet's moving field makes swirls of current in the pipe.
Those currents make their own field that pushes back.

new.q: A compass is placed near a wire. When the current direction is reversed, the needle:
new.w: The field direction around a wire follows the current direction.
sol: Right-hand rule: thumb with the current.
Flip the thumb, and the fingers' curl flips too.

new.q: Two long parallel wires carry current in the SAME direction. They:
new.w: Same-direction currents attract; opposite-direction currents repel.
sol: Each wire's field acts on the other's current.
Remember: parallel currents attract (opposite of like charges!).

new.q: An electromagnet's current is doubled with the same coil. Its field becomes about:
new.w: Field grows with the current.
sol: More current means more circling field.
Too much current heats the wire.

new.q: Electromagnet A has 50 turns and 1.0 A; electromagnet B has 100 turns and 0.5 A, same size and core. Compare their strengths.
o: About equal, since turns × current is the same
new.w: Strength follows ampere-turns (turns × current).

new.q: Why does the wire in a homemade electromagnet get warm?
o: Current through the wire's resistance makes heat (P = I²R)
new.w: Any current in a resistor makes heat.
sol: A warm battery and wire are warnings.

new.q: A generator coil of 100 turns induces 0.50 V when spun at a certain speed. The same motion with a 300-turn coil gives how many volts?
new.w: Induced voltage is proportional to the number of turns.
sol: Each turn adds its own small voltage in series.
3 times the turns means 3 times the volts.

new.q: A power line has 2.0 Ω resistance and carries 10 kW. At 1000 V, the current is 10 A. How many watts are lost in the line?
new.w: Line loss is I²R.

new.q: The same 10 kW is sent through the same line, but the voltage is raised 10 times by a transformer. The line loss becomes:
new.w: Higher voltage means lower current, and loss goes as the current squared.
sol: That is why power lines use high voltage: less lost as heat.

new.q: The job of a commutator in a DC motor is to:
o: reverse the coil current every half turn so the torque keeps the same direction
new.w: Without reversal, the coil would just stop after a half turn.
sol: The coil is pulled around until it lines up, then the current flips.

new.q: Match each device to what it does.
pairs: Magnet that can be switched off
new.w: Each uses the link between electricity and magnetism.

new.q: Order the steps in a simple generator.
items: The coil moves through the field
The magnetic flux through the coil changes
new.w: Faraday's law links changing flux to voltage.
sol: emf pushes current in a closed circuit.

new.q: Select ALL that a magnet attracts strongly.
new.w: Iron, nickel, cobalt and steel (iron-based) are ferromagnetic.
sol: Copper and aluminum are not attracted.

new.q: Why use a soft iron core in an electromagnet rather than hard steel?
o: Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current stops
new.w: The magnet can then be switched off.
sol: Soft iron magnetizes easily and demagnetizes easily.
Hard steel stays magnetized, like a permanent magnet.

new.q: A relay is mainly made from:
o: an electromagnet that moves a switch
new.w: A small coil current switches a larger one.
sol: Like a light finger on a big switch.

new.q: Which sets how much voltage a magnet moving past a coil induces?
o: How long the wire is not moving
The length of the lead wires only
new.w: Faraday: emf = turns × rate of change of flux.
sol: Faster motion means a faster change.

new.q: A permanent magnet can be weakened by:
o: strong heating or repeated hard hits
new.w: Heat and shock jumble the tiny magnetic regions (domains).
sol: Domains are tiny areas all pointing the same way.
Heat or hammering knocks them out of line.
Like a neat marching band scattered.

report: Diode: 7 numeric answers had SI values under mA/mW/mJ/µF units (fixed); diode-012 zero-valued numeric converted to mcq; deleted 3 numeric families with the same unit bug (plus duplicate 057/069 templates) and cap-e, cap-s families, replaced by new items. Mag: deleted 11 near-identical classification items and 2 duplicates (035, 037), ferrite called ferromagnetic (it is ferrimagnetic). Added 101 new items (diode, cap, mag), about 50% level 3. Doubts: mag topic is outside 2027 text per note; Zener/RC/bridge items are extensions beyond the study note; unseen family members (ledstd, xfmr, 027) not individually checked.
